beats.say: A blast flattened a forest in Siberia, and left no crater.
beats.headline: WHAT EXPLODED?
beats.short_title: What REALLY Exploded Over Tunguska? 💥 Case #28 Meatball Investigates
beats.comment: What do you think it was? ☄️ space rock / 🛸 UFO
beats.bonus: On 30 June 1908 an explosion over the Podkamennaya Tunguska River in Siberia flattened about 80 million trees over roughly 2,150 square kilometres. No impact crater was found, because a space rock most likely exploded in the air (an airburst). Leonid Kulik's expedition reached the site in 1927.
beats.caption: In 1908 something flattened 80 million trees in Siberia and left no crater.
sources: Wikipedia, Tunguska event: 30 June 1908 airburst over the Podkamennaya Tunguska River; about 80 million trees flattened over about 2,150 km²; no impact crater; Leonid Kulik's expeditions (first 1921, reached the site 1927) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunguska_event (checked 2026-10-26)
NASA Science, 'The Tunguska Impact – 100 Years Later' (2008) — https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/planetary-science/30jun_tunguska/

beats.headline: PSYCHIC SPIES?
beats.short_title: The US Really Had Psychic Spies 🔮 Case #29 Meatball Investigates
beats.comment: Would you trust a psychic spy? 🔮 yes / 🙄 no
beats.bonus: The Stargate Project: from 1978 to 1995 a small US Army and Defense Intelligence Agency unit at Fort Meade tried 'remote viewing', describing distant targets with the mind. It was declassified in 1995 after a CIA-commissioned review found it had never been useful in any intelligence operation. Total cost: about $20 million.
beats.caption: The US government really paid for psychic spies.
sources: Wikipedia, Stargate Project: US Army/DIA unit at Fort Meade (from 1978 as Grill Flame) investigating psychic 'remote viewing' for intelligence; terminated and declassified in 1995 after a CIA-commissioned review concluded it was never useful in any intelligence operation; about $20 million; featured in 'The Men Who Stare at Goats' (2004 book, 2009 film) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stargate_Project_(U.S._Army_unit) (checked 2026-10-26)
American Institutes for Research, 'An Evaluation of Remote Viewing: Research and Applications' (1995), commissioned by the CIA

Parliament soaked its curtains in chemicals, because the river smelled that bad.
beats.headline: PARLIAMENT VS A SMELL?
beats.short_title: The Great Stink of 1858 Was REAL 🤢 Case #30 Meatball Investigates
beats.comment: Could you handle the smell? 🤢 yes / 🤮 no way
beats.bonus: In the hot summer of 1858 the Thames, full of untreated sewage, smelled so bad that Parliament's riverside curtains were soaked in chloride of lime. The 'Great Stink' finally pushed through Joseph Bazalgette's plan for London's sewers and embankments, including about 1,100 miles of street sewers.
beats.caption: In 1858 London's river smelled so bad it changed the city forever.
sources: Wikipedia, Great Stink: July-August 1858, Central London; hot weather and untreated sewage in the Thames; Parliament's riverside curtains soaked in lime chloride; led to Joseph Bazalgette's sewer system and the Victoria, Chelsea and Albert Embankments, with about 1,100 miles of street sewers — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Stink (checked 2026-10-26)

beats.headline: NOBODY CAN READ IT?
beats.short_title: The Voynich Manuscript: The Book Nobody Can Read 📜 Case #31
beats.comment: Do you think it means something? 📜 yes / 🤡 gibberish
beats.bonus: The Voynich manuscript is a 15th-century book (its vellum is radiocarbon-dated to 1404-1438) written in an unknown script, full of unidentified plants and strange drawings. Top codebreakers, including those who cracked wartime codes, have failed to read it. It is held at Yale's Beinecke Library and is named after Wilfrid Voynich, who bought it in 1912.
beats.caption: A 600-year-old book nobody can read.
sources: Wikipedia, Voynich manuscript: illustrated codex in an unknown script; vellum radiocarbon-dated (University of Arizona, 2009) to 1404-1438; held by Yale's Beinecke Library (MS 408); codebreakers including William and Elizebeth Friedman, Prescott Currier and John Tiltman failed to read it; named after book dealer Wilfrid Voynich, who bought it in 1912 — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voynich_manuscript (checked 2026-10-26)
Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University, MS 408 (digitized facsimile)

A broke businessman declared himself Emperor of the United States.
beats.headline: AN AMERICAN EMPEROR?
beats.short_title: America Had an EMPEROR. Really. 👑 Case #32 Meatball Investigates
beats.comment: Would you have bowed? 👑 yes / 🙅 no
beats.bonus: In 1859 Joshua Norton, a San Francisco businessman who had lost his fortune, proclaimed himself 'Emperor of the United States'. San Francisco played along for 21 years: he issued his own currency, which some businesses accepted, and decreed things like abolishing Congress and building a bridge across the bay, which opened in 1936. Thousands attended his funeral in 1880.
beats.caption: San Francisco had its own self-declared emperor for 21 years.
sources: Wikipedia, Emperor Norton: Joshua Abraham Norton (1818-1880) declared himself Emperor of the United States in 1859; decreed the abolition of Congress (12 Oct 1859); proposed a bridge across San Francisco Bay (the Bay Bridge opened 1936); issued currency honored by some establishments; large public funeral in January 1880 — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Norton (checked 2026-10-26)
William Drury, 'Norton I, Emperor of the United States' (Dodd, Mead, 1986)

beats.headline: FAKE PLANS?
beats.short_title: Operation Mincemeat: The Dead Man Who Fooled Hitler 🕵️ Case #33
beats.comment: Would you have fallen for it? 🕵️ yes / 🧐 no
beats.bonus: Operation Mincemeat (1943): British intelligence officers Ewen Montagu and Charles Cholmondeley dressed a dead man as 'Major William Martin' and floated him off Huelva, Spain, carrying fake letters saying the Allies would invade Greece and Sardinia. The Germans believed it, and the real target was Sicily. The man's real name, Glyndwr Michael, was confirmed in 1996.
beats.caption: A dead man with fake plans fooled the Germans in 1943.
sources: Wikipedia, Operation Mincemeat: 1943 British deception; Ewen Montagu and Charles Cholmondeley dressed the body of Glyndwr Michael as 'Major William Martin', Royal Marines, with fake letters suggesting the Allies would invade Greece and Sardinia rather than Sicily; released from HMS Seraph off Huelva, Spain; the Germans believed it; the corpse's identity was uncovered in 1996 by historian Roger Morgan — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Mincemeat (checked 2026-10-26)
